screens.title: Redis Replication: The Foundation of High Availability
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn what Redis replication actually does, why it is the foundation for scaling reads and improving availability, and how a simple master and multiple replicas work together in practice. We'll start by defining the master‑replica relationship, then walk through the initial full synchronization that uses an RDB snapshot and buffered commands, and finally show how the system streams writes asynchronously so the master stays fast. You will also see concrete configuration examples using the REPLICAOF command and a hands‑on lab that runs a master and two replicas on different ports. Along the way, we'll explain how to monitor replication health with the INFO replication command and why the replication offset matters when checking lag. I will point out common mistakes people make, such as forgetting to set replicaof in the configuration or trying to write to a read‑only replica, and explain the practical consequence of asynchronous replication when a master fails. By the end you'll understand how replication supports read scaling, redundancy, and the tradeoffs between performance and potential short windows of data divergence.

Redis Replication: The Foundation of High Availability

Understand how a single master streams updates to replicas, how the initial RDB sync works, and why asynchronous replication is a deliberate tradeoff for performance.

In this lesson
Master, initial sync, and ongoing replication.
Coming up
Hands‑on setup with REPLICAOF and INFO replication.
Why it matters
Scale reads, increase redundancy, and enable smoother maintenance.
Concept snapshot
Master accepts writes; replicas serve reads and mirror the dataset.
Initial RDB snapshot then buffered commands for catch-up.
Ongoing asynchronous streaming of commands.
Explore Key Topics

Start with architecture, then configuration, then monitoring to complete the replication workflow.

Configuration: REPLICAOF, redis.conf, replica-read-only setting.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain and configure basic Redis master‑replica replication, use the REPLICAOF command or redis. conf to connect replicas to a master, and monitor replication health with the CLI. You will practice creating an initial synchronization, observing how the master snapshots data and buffers commands while a replica catches up, and interpret the INFO replication output to detect lag using the replication offset. These are practical skills: you will deploy a master and two replicas, verify data flows by setting keys on the master and reading from replicas, and intentionally observe the error that occurs when attempting to write to a read‑only replica. Understanding the asynchronous nature of replication is critical; it explains why a master can be fast and why there is a small window of potential data divergence. Finally, you will learn common troubleshooting checks such as ensuring replicaof settings are present, checking firewall and network connectivity, and keeping persistence enabled on the master so that a restart doesn't lose data. These objectives prepare you to scale reads, add redundancy, and recognize when to use external failover tools.

screens.title: Master‑Replica Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Master‑replica architecture is the structural core of Redis replication. The master is the authoritative source for all write operations. Replicas connect to the master and maintain copies of the dataset, serving read requests and reducing load on the master. This separation matters because it lets the master focus on fast writes while replicas handle parallel read traffic, improving throughput without complex coordination. A concrete example: an application writes session state to the master. Many web servers read session data; routing their GET requests to replicas spreads the read load and prevents the master from becoming a bottleneck. A common misconception is to think replicas are instantaneous mirrors; because replication is asynchronous, replicas can lag briefly behind the master, so reads from a replica might return slightly stale data. Another misconception is to treat replicas as automatic failover masters — replication itself does not promote a replica. Promotion requires manual action or an external system like Redis Sentinel. The takeaway: architecture clarifies where to send writes and reads, and it defines operational expectations for consistency and failover. Ask yourself which operations in your application can tolerate slightly stale reads and which must always go to the master.

keyIdea.title: Architecture insight
keyIdea.text: Master handles writes; replicas mirror data and serve reads. This tradeoff improves performance but accepts brief windows of staleness.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Master‑Replica Architecture
Definition

A master accepts all writes and streams updates to connected replicas. Replicas apply those updates and serve read requests. This design separates write responsibility from read scaling and redundancy.

Master: authoritative writer, produces RDB snapshots and streams commands.
Replica: receives snapshot, replays buffered and streamed commands, serves reads.
Use case: scale many read clients by distributing reads to replicas.
Example scenario
A web app writes user profile updates to the master. Multiple web servers read profile data from replicas to reduce latency and protect the master from read spikes. If the replica lag is small, most reads return fresh data; if the replica lags, read operations may see slightly stale profiles.
Check your understanding
Which operations must always go to the master to guarantee immediately visible writes? Write operations that require immediate visibility.
Common mistake
Treating replicas as instant backups and relying on them for strong consistency.
Pro tip
Route writes to master and send idempotent or eventually consistent reads to replicas.
Key Takeaway
Architecture defines where to send different traffic to balance performance and consistency.

screens.title: Initial Full Synchronization
screens.narratorSegment: Initial synchronization is the handshake that brings a new replica up to date. When a replica first connects, the master creates a background RDB snapshot of the entire dataset and sends it to the replica as a bulk transfer. While this transfer is in progress the master buffers all incoming write commands. After the replica receives and loads the RDB file, the master streams the buffered commands so the replica can replay them in order and reach the current state. A concrete example: suppose your master holds sessions and you add a replica. The replica receives the RDB snapshot containing current sessions, then the master replays buffered SET commands that occurred during the transfer so the replica ends up identical to the master's data. A common misconception is that partial resynchronization will always handle all disconnects; initial full sync is required when the replica lacks an acceptable backlog window. The takeaway is that the full sync is efficient and automatic, but it requires enough disk and network capacity for the snapshot transfer. Always monitor transfers during large datasets to avoid prolonged buffering that could increase memory use on the master.

keyIdea.title: Full sync summary
keyIdea.text: Master sends an RDB snapshot and buffered writes; replica loads snapshot then replays buffered commands to catch up.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Initial Full Synchronization
Step-by-step
1. Replica connects and requests a sync. Master starts RDB snapshot generation.
2. Master transfers RDB snapshot to replica as a bulk file while buffering new writes.
3. Replica loads snapshot into memory and then requests buffered commands.
4. Master sends buffered writes; replica replays them and becomes current.
Concrete example

You add a replica to a system with many session keys. Master snapshots the dataset and sends the dump. Writes while the dump is sent are buffered; after loading the dump the replica replays buffered SETs and appears identical to the master.

Common mistake
Not accounting for memory used by the master to buffer commands during long snapshot transfers, which may cause increased memory pressure.
When to watch
Monitor snapshot duration for large datasets; long transfers increase buffered commands and memory use.
Pro tip
Use persistence tuning and network capacity planning to shorten snapshot time where needed.
Key Takeaway
Full sync guarantees an identical dataset by snapshot + buffered commands, but watch transfer time and buffering effects.

screens.title: Ongoing Replication: Streaming Commands
screens.narratorSegment: After a replica completes initial synchronization, the master switches to continuously streaming subsequent write commands to all connected replicas. This streaming is the mechanism that keeps replicas up to date in near real time. The master emits each write as it is accepted, and replicas apply those commands in the same order to preserve dataset consistency. Because the stream is asynchronous, the master does not wait for a replica to acknowledge a command before processing the next write. A concrete example: after you SET a key on the master, that SET is streamed to replicas and they apply it promptly; however, if a network blip delays delivery, the replica may be briefly behind. A common misconception is that streaming provides synchronous durability; it does not. Streaming prioritizes master speed and low write latency, accepting a small window where recent writes may not yet be on all replicas. The practical implication is to design applications that can tolerate slightly stale reads or direct critical writes to the master. Monitoring offsets and link status helps you detect when streaming is lagging. Ongoing Replication: Streaming Commands means ongoing replication streams write commands in real time; asynchronous streaming favors master performance at the cost of potential short-term divergence.. In practical terms, how the master streams writes to replicas after sync. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Streaming Commands
How streaming works

Once a replica is caught up, the master streams real-time write commands to that replica. Commands are sent in order and applied by the replica to maintain consistency with the master.

Asynchronous: the master does not wait for acknowledgement. This design keeps write performance high.
Concrete example

You issue SET session:123 "stateA" on the master. The master streams the SET and replicas apply it. If network latency affects delivery, the replica may apply the SET milliseconds later and briefly show older state.

Misconception check
Streaming is not synchronous replication; it does not guarantee the replica has the write before the master continues.
When this matters
Systems needing immediate global consistency should direct critical writes to the master or use additional coordination.
Pro tip
Design reads that tolerate slight staleness or implement read‑after‑write to the master for critical paths.
Key Takeaway
Streaming keeps replicas near real-time while keeping the master responsive, but it is not a synchronous durability guarantee.

screens.title: Configuring Replication with REPLICAOF
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a replica is straightforward and can be done at runtime or in the configuration file. The command REPLICAOF master_host master_port tells a Redis instance to become a replica of the specified master. Alternatively you can add replicaof master_host master_port to the instance's redis. conf so it joins the master at startup. A concrete hands-on example: if your master runs on 127.0.0.1 port 6379, run REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379 in redis‑cli on the replica, or add replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379 to redis-replica. conf and restart the replica server. Remember that replicas are read-only by default; attempts to SET keys on a replica will fail with an error. A misconception to avoid is believing older slaveof syntax is recommended — REPLICAOF is the preferred, explicit command name in modern versions. The practical tip is to script your redis. conf templates for master and replicas and verify the replica connection with INFO replication after starting both instances. This ensures repeatable deployments in testing and production. Configuring Replication with REPLICAOF means use replicaof at runtime or replicaof in redis.conf; replicas default to read-only to prevent data divergence.. In practical terms, using replicaof and redis.conf to add replicas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Configuring Replicas
Command example
# On the replica's redis-cli
REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379
This tells the running instance to connect to the master and begin synchronization immediately.
Configuration file example
# redis-replica1.conf
port 6380
replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379
daemonize yes
Putting replicaof in redis.conf makes the replica join automatically on restart.
Misconception
Don't assume REPLICAOF will configure persistence or network rules; those are separate concerns.
Pro tip
Script your configs so each instance has predictable ports, data dirs, and replicaof settings for reproducible labs.
Key Takeaway
REPLICAOF and replicaof are the primary mechanisms to attach a replica to a master; verify the connection with INFO replication.

screens.title: Replica Read‑Only Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: By default a Redis replica is read-only, which prevents clients from executing write commands against it. This safeguard reduces the risk of divergence between the master and replica datasets. If you attempt to SET a key on a replica with replica-read-only yes, Redis will return an error and refuse the write. A concrete example: in a replicated environment, a web server misconfigured to send a SET to a replica will see an error instead of silently diverging the dataset. Some operators may be tempted to disable read‑only mode by setting replica-read-only no to allow local writes on a replica. That is generally discouraged because it breaks the replication guarantee and makes recovery and failover much more complex. A helpful contrast: writable replicas may act like independent masters, but that creates conflicting updates and inconsistency. The takeaway is to keep replicas read-only in most production uses, and if you must accept writes on a replica for a special workflow, plan for reconciliation and understand the risk of divergence. Ask yourself whether local writes are worth the increased complexity. Replica Read‑Only Behavior means replicas are read-only by default to avoid divergence; disabling read-only allows writes but introduces complex consistency problems.. In practical terms, why replicas prevent writes by default and the implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Replica Read‑Only Behavior
Default behavior

Replicas refuse write commands when replica-read-only is enabled. This preserves a single authoritative source of writes and prevents unintended divergence.

Example
# Attempting this on a replica:
SET somekey "value"
# will return an error when replica-read-only is yes
Comparison
Writable replica: allows local writes, risks divergence and complex recovery.
Read-only replica: consistent mirror of master writes, safer for scaling reads.
If you decide to allow writes on a replica, treat it as a deliberate architectural choice and implement reconciliation strategies.
Common mistake
Disabling read-only without a plan for reconciling conflicting writes across replicas.
Pro tip
Keep replicas read-only and route critical writes to the master to preserve a simple, reliable model.
Key Takeaway
Read-only replicas avoid divergence; writable replicas add complexity and are usually discouraged.

screens.title: Monitoring Replication with INFO replication
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring replication health is essential to detect lag or disconnects before they impact user experience. The INFO replication command returns a structured set of fields. For a master you'll see role:master and connected_slaves with details for each replica. For a replica you'll see role:replica, master_host, master_port, master_link_status, and client information about its link. The replication offset is a key metric: it expresses how many bytes of replication stream have been processed and lets you compare master and replica offsets to estimate lag. A concrete example: if the master shows master_repl_offset of 102400 and a replica shows master_repl_offset of 102000, the replica is 400 bytes behind. A common misconception is to read offset alone as a precise time metric; offset measures bytes processed and is a proxy for lag but must be interpreted with workload characteristics. The practical check: regularly sample offsets and master_link_status. If a replica's master_link_status is down or offset difference grows, investigate network, C P U, or input and output contention. Use this data to decide whether to rebalance reads or promote a replica under controlled conditions with external tooling.

Sample INFO replication (master)

connected_slaves:2
slave0:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6380,state=online,offset=102400,lag=0

Sample INFO replication (replica)

Interpretation
Compare master_repl_offset values to estimate bytes of lag. Use this with load patterns to understand real impact.
Misconception
Offset difference is not a direct time measure; it should be correlated with observed delays and throughput.
Key Takeaway
INFO replication is the first-line tool to detect replication lag and link problems; monitor offsets and link status regularly.

screens.title: Partial Resynchronization and Replication Backlog
screens.narratorSegment: Partial resynchronization is a performance optimization that avoids a full RDB transfer when a replica reconnects after a short disconnect. Redis maintains a replication backlog buffer on the master: a ring buffer holding recent write commands. If a replica temporarily loses connection but attempts to resynchronize before the backlog has cycled out the missing commands, the master can send only the missing commands and the replica quickly catches up without a full snapshot. A concrete example: if a replica loses network connectivity for a second and reconnects, rather than redoing the whole RDB snapshot, it requests the missing range from the master's backlog and resumes streaming. A common misconception is that partial resync always works; if the backlog no longer contains the needed commands because the disconnection lasted too long, the master will fall back to a full synchronization. The takeaway: configure an appropriate backlog size that fits your workload and expected transient outages, monitor for frequent full syncs as a signal that backlog is too small or disconnects are too long, and understand that partial resynchronization reduces load and speeds recovery when possible.

keyIdea.text: If missing commands remain in the master's replication backlog, a replica can partially resynchronize by fetching only those commands instead of receiving a full RDB snapshot.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Partial Resynchronization
What is the replication backlog?

A circular buffer on the master that stores recent write commands. Its size determines how long a disconnected replica can catch up using only the backlog.

Partial resync when backlog contains missing commands
Concrete example

Replica disconnects for a short interval. On reconnect it requests commands starting at its last processed offset. If those commands remain in the backlog, the master sends them and the replica resumes without an RDB snapshot.

If the disconnect was long and backlog no longer contains required commands, the master will send a full RDB snapshot and buffered commands instead.
When to tune
Increase backlog if transient disconnects are common and full syncs cause operational pain.
Misconception
Partial resync is not guaranteed; it depends on backlog retention and disconnect duration.
Key Takeaway
Partial resynchronization speeds recovery by using a backlog, but backlog size and disconnect duration determine success.

screens.title: Read Scaling and Data Redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: Replicas serve two primary operational purposes: read scaling and redundancy. For read scaling, place read-heavy operations on replicas so the master can handle writes without extra load. An example is caching user profiles: the master handles writes from user updates while replicas answer many read requests from many clients in parallel. For redundancy, replicas hold copies of the dataset so that if the master fails, a replica can be promoted to reduce downtime. It's important to note that replication alone does not provide automatic failover, but it does provide the copies Sentinel or external orchestrators need to promote a replacement master. A common misconception is to assume more replicas always increase safety; while replicas add redundancy, they also increase network traffic and can amplify replication lag if the master is overloaded. The practical guidance: use replicas to distribute read traffic and maintain enough replicas in diverse failure domains for redundancy, while ensuring you have external failover or a manual promotion plan and persistence enabled on the master. Consider what level of staleness your application can tolerate when routing reads to replicas.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Read Scaling & Redundancy
Read scaling

Distribute read traffic across multiple replicas to increase throughput and reduce latency. This is especially useful for read-heavy caches and analytics queries that can tolerate slightly stale data.

Use replicas for reads
Data redundancy

Replicas maintain copies of the dataset so you can recover more quickly from a master failure. To automate failover you need additional tooling; replication alone only provides the copies.

When to replicate
When read demand exceeds a single server's capacity or when you need dataset copies across failure domains.
Caveat
Replicas can lag; route only reads that can tolerate slight staleness unless you implement strong routing rules.
Key Takeaway
Use replicas to scale reads and provide copies for recovery, but pair them with failover tooling and persistence to ensure safety.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Persistence Advice
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes cause replication issues. Developers sometimes forget to set replicaof in redis. conf, leaving an instance running as a master unintentionally. Another frequent error is attempting to write to a replica without understanding replica-read-only behavior; such writes fail, which can confuse application logic. Network connectivity and firewall rules are leading operational causes of replicas falling behind or disconnecting altogether. For safety, always enable persistence on the master — either RDB, AOF, or both — so that if all nodes go down you can restore from durable storage. A concrete example: if your master lacks persistence and experiences a crash during a power outage, replicas only mirror the master's in-memory state; without persistence the master's dataset may be unrecoverable after restart. Use INFO replication to detect disconnected replicas and rising replication offsets as early warnings. The takeaway is to validate configuration files before starting instances, ensure proper networking, enable master persistence, and plan for automated failover using external tools if you need minimal downtime. Ask yourself: do I have monitoring and a promotion plan ready for an unexpected master outage?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Troubleshooting & Persistence
Checklist of common mistakes
  • Forgetting replicaof so instance starts as master.
  • Attempting writes on read-only replicas and not handling errors.
  • Firewall or routing blocking replication ports between master and replicas.
Persistence advice

Enable RDB or AOF on the master so that a restart does not lose the authoritative dataset. Replicas mirror in-memory state but rely on the master's persistence for full recovery after total outages.

When to act
If INFO replication shows master_link_status:down or rising offset diffs, investigate network and replica performance immediately.
Pro tip
Automate configuration deployment and health checks to avoid human errors like missing replicaof lines.
Key Takeaway
Operational hygiene—correct configs, enabled persistence, and network checks—prevents most replication failures.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the key concepts you should carry forward. First, master‑replica architecture separates write responsibility from read scalability: the master accepts writes and replicas mirror the dataset to serve reads. Second, replication is asynchronous; this design favors master performance and introduces a small possibility of short windows of divergence. Third, initial full synchronization uses an RDB snapshot and buffered commands, while partial resynchronization can avoid full snapshots when the master's backlog still contains missing commands. Keep an eye on INFO replication output to read roles, master_link_status, and replication offsets to detect lag. In practice, configure replicas with REPLICAOF or redis. conf replicaof, keep replicas read-only in most cases, enable persistence on the master, and plan failover with external tools. These concepts combine into a practical approach: use replicas to scale reads and provide redundancy, but monitor and plan to manage consistency and recovery. Master handles writes; replicas mirror and serve reads for scaling and redundancy.

Master streams commands and does not wait for replica acknowledgements, favoring performance over immediate global durability.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn what Redis replication actually does, why it is the foundation for scaling reads and improving availability, and how a simple master and multiple replicas work together in practice. We'll start by defining the master‑replica relationship, then walk through the initial full synchronization that uses an RDB snapshot and buffered commands, and finally show how the system streams writes asynchronously so the master stays fast. You will also see concrete configuration examples using the REPLICAOF command and a hands‑on lab that runs a master and two replicas on different ports. Along the way, we'll explain how to monitor replication health with the INFO replication command and why the replication offset matters when checking lag. I will point out common mistakes people make, such as forgetting to set replicaof in the configuration or trying to write to a read‑only replica, and explain the practical consequence of asynchronous replication when a master fails. By the end you'll understand how replication supports read scaling, redundancy, and the tradeoffs between performance and potential short windows of data divergence.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain and configure basic Redis master‑replica replication, use the REPLICAOF command or redis. conf to connect replicas to a master, and monitor replication health with the CLI. You will practice creating an initial synchronization, observing how the master snapshots data and buffers commands while a replica catches up, and interpret the INFO replication output to detect lag using the replication offset. These are practical skills: you will deploy a master and two replicas, verify data flows by setting keys on the master and reading from replicas, and intentionally observe the error that occurs when attempting to write to a read‑only replica. Understanding the asynchronous nature of replication is critical; it explains why a master can be fast and why there is a small window of potential data divergence. Finally, you will learn common troubleshooting checks such as ensuring replicaof settings are present, checking firewall and network connectivity, and keeping persistence enabled on the master so that a restart doesn't lose data. These objectives prepare you to scale reads, add redundancy, and recognize when to use external failover tools.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical skills and diagnostics. You will start a master and two replicas locally, add a key on the master, and confirm the replicas receive it. You will run INFO replication on both master and replica and learn to read the role, connected replicas, master_host, and master_link_status fields. You will also test the expected error when attempting to set a key on a read‑only replica. These tasks are concrete: create redis‑server config files for each instance, run redis‑server with those files, and use redis‑cli to interact. Monitoring exercises include reading the replication offset and comparing offsets across instances to estimate lag. You will also practice checking network and firewall settings as common causes for replication failure. By building and observing this simple cluster, you'll gain confidence that you can both configure replication and recognize operational issues when they arise.

Master‑replica architecture is the structural core of Redis replication. The master is the authoritative source for all write operations. Replicas connect to the master and maintain copies of the dataset, serving read requests and reducing load on the master. This separation matters because it lets the master focus on fast writes while replicas handle parallel read traffic, improving throughput without complex coordination. A concrete example: an application writes session state to the master. Many web servers read session data; routing their GET requests to replicas spreads the read load and prevents the master from becoming a bottleneck. A common misconception is to think replicas are instantaneous mirrors; because replication is asynchronous, replicas can lag briefly behind the master, so reads from a replica might return slightly stale data. Another misconception is to treat replicas as automatic failover masters — replication itself does not promote a replica. Promotion requires manual action or an external system like Redis Sentinel. The takeaway: architecture clarifies where to send writes and reads, and it defines operational expectations for consistency and failover. Ask yourself which operations in your application can tolerate slightly stale reads and which must always go to the master.

Initial synchronization is the handshake that brings a new replica up to date. When a replica first connects, the master creates a background RDB snapshot of the entire dataset and sends it to the replica as a bulk transfer. While this transfer is in progress the master buffers all incoming write commands. After the replica receives and loads the RDB file, the master streams the buffered commands so the replica can replay them in order and reach the current state. A concrete example: suppose your master holds sessions and you add a replica. The replica receives the RDB snapshot containing current sessions, then the master replays buffered SET commands that occurred during the transfer so the replica ends up identical to the master's data. A common misconception is that partial resynchronization will always handle all disconnects; initial full sync is required when the replica lacks an acceptable backlog window. The takeaway is that the full sync is efficient and automatic, but it requires enough disk and network capacity for the snapshot transfer. Always monitor transfers during large datasets to avoid prolonged buffering that could increase memory use on the master.

After a replica completes initial synchronization, the master switches to continuously streaming subsequent write commands to all connected replicas. This streaming is the mechanism that keeps replicas up to date in near real time. The master emits each write as it is accepted, and replicas apply those commands in the same order to preserve dataset consistency. Because the stream is asynchronous, the master does not wait for a replica to acknowledge a command before processing the next write. A concrete example: after you SET a key on the master, that SET is streamed to replicas and they apply it promptly; however, if a network blip delays delivery, the replica may be briefly behind. A common misconception is that streaming provides synchronous durability; it does not. Streaming prioritizes master speed and low write latency, accepting a small window where recent writes may not yet be on all replicas. The practical implication is to design applications that can tolerate slightly stale reads or direct critical writes to the master. Monitoring offsets and link status helps you detect when streaming is lagging. Ongoing Replication: Streaming Commands means ongoing replication streams write commands in real time; asynchronous streaming favors master performance at the cost of potential short-term divergence.. In practical terms, how the master streams writes to replicas after sync. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Configuring a replica is straightforward and can be done at runtime or in the configuration file. The command REPLICAOF master_host master_port tells a Redis instance to become a replica of the specified master. Alternatively you can add replicaof master_host master_port to the instance's redis. conf so it joins the master at startup. A concrete hands-on example: if your master runs on 127.0.0.1 port 6379, run REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379 in redis‑cli on the replica, or add replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379 to redis-replica. conf and restart the replica server. Remember that replicas are read-only by default; attempts to SET keys on a replica will fail with an error. A misconception to avoid is believing older slaveof syntax is recommended — REPLICAOF is the preferred, explicit command name in modern versions. The practical tip is to script your redis. conf templates for master and replicas and verify the replica connection with INFO replication after starting both instances. This ensures repeatable deployments in testing and production. By default a Redis replica is read-only, which prevents clients from executing write commands against it. This safeguard reduces the risk of divergence between the master and replica datasets. If you attempt to SET a key on a replica with replica-read-only yes, Redis will return an error and refuse the write. A concrete example: in a replicated environment, a web server misconfigured to send a SET to a replica will see an error instead of silently diverging the dataset. That is generally discouraged because it breaks the replication guarantee and makes recovery and failover much more complex. A helpful contrast: writable replicas may act like independent masters, but that creates conflicting updates and inconsistency. The takeaway is to keep replicas read-only in most production uses, and if you must accept writes on a replica for a special workflow, plan for reconciliation and understand the risk of divergence. Ask yourself whether local writes are worth the increased complexity. Replicas serve two primary operational purposes: read scaling and redundancy. For read scaling, place read-heavy operations on replicas so the master can handle writes without extra load. An example is caching user profiles: the master handles writes from user updates while replicas answer many read requests from many clients in parallel. For redundancy, replicas hold copies of the dataset so that if the master fails, a replica can be promoted to reduce downtime. It's important to note that replication alone does not provide automatic failover, but it does provide the copies Sentinel or external orchestrators need to promote a replacement master. A common misconception is to assume more replicas always increase safety; while replicas add redundancy, they also increase network traffic and can amplify replication lag if the master is overloaded. The practical guidance: use replicas to distribute read traffic and maintain enough replicas in diverse failure domains for redundancy, while ensuring you have external failover or a manual promotion plan and persistence enabled on the master. Consider what level of staleness your application can tolerate when routing reads to replicas.

Several common mistakes cause replication issues. Developers sometimes forget to set replicaof in redis. conf, leaving an instance running as a master unintentionally. Another frequent error is attempting to write to a replica without understanding replica-read-only behavior; such writes fail, which can confuse application logic. Network connectivity and firewall rules are leading operational causes of replicas falling behind or disconnecting altogether. For safety, always enable persistence on the master — either RDB, AOF, or both — so that if all nodes go down you can restore from durable storage. A concrete example: if your master lacks persistence and experiences a crash during a power outage, replicas only mirror the master's in-memory state; without persistence the master's dataset may be unrecoverable after restart. Use INFO replication to detect disconnected replicas and rising replication offsets as early warnings. The takeaway is to validate configuration files before starting instances, ensure proper networking, enable master persistence, and plan for automated failover using external tools if you need minimal downtime. Ask yourself: do I have monitoring and a promotion plan ready for an unexpected master outage?

Let's summarize the key concepts you should carry forward. First, master‑replica architecture separates write responsibility from read scalability: the master accepts writes and replicas mirror the dataset to serve reads. Second, replication is asynchronous; this design favors master performance and introduces a small possibility of short windows of divergence. Third, initial full synchronization uses an RDB snapshot and buffered commands, while partial resynchronization can avoid full snapshots when the master's backlog still contains missing commands. Keep an eye on INFO replication output to read roles, master_link_status, and replication offsets to detect lag. In practice, configure replicas with REPLICAOF or redis. conf replicaof, keep replicas read-only in most cases, enable persistence on the master, and plan failover with external tools. These concepts combine into a practical approach: use replicas to scale reads and provide redundancy, but monitor and plan to manage consistency and recovery.
